Lesson A0-01: Understanding Dutch Sounds and Spelling ​

Level: A0 (Foundations)
CEFR Level: A0
Duration: 90 minutes
New Vocabulary: 32 words
Grammar Focus: Alphabet, vowel sounds, diphthongs, word stress

1. Lesson Goal ​

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to read the Dutch alphabet aloud, distinguish between long and short vowel sounds, recognize and pronounce diphthongs (ui, ou, au, ei, ij), identify word stress patterns, and read simple Dutch words with reasonable pronunciation.

2. Previous Knowledge ​

This is the first lesson in the curriculum. No prior Dutch knowledge is required.

If you're returning to learn Dutch after some time, review the English alphabet to refresh your memory -- we'll be using the same 26 letters, but with different names and sounds.

3. Why This Matters ​

Dutch pronunciation may seem difficult at first, but it follows clear rules. Unlike English -- where words like "tough," "through," and "though" all have different pronunciations -- Dutch pronunciation is much more predictable once you learn the patterns.

Mastering pronunciation now means:

  • You'll read new words correctly without memorizing how to say each one
  • You'll spell words correctly by understanding sound-spelling patterns
  • You'll be understood when you speak
  • You'll recognize words when you hear them

This foundation is essential before learning grammar and vocabulary.

4. Grammar ​

Dutch uses the same 26-letter alphabet as English, but the letter names and sound-spelling patterns are different.

The Alphabet ​

Dutch letter names are pronounced like this:

LetterDutch NamePronunciationNote
AahAHlike "father"
BbeBAYsimilar to English
CceSAYoften S before e/i, K elsewhere
DdeDAYfinal D often sounds like T
EeAYlike "say," shorter
FefEFfamiliar
GgeKHAYthroat sound (like rough "loch")
HhaHAHpronounced clearly
IiEElike "see"
JjeYAYlike English Y
KkaKAHno strong puff of air
LelELfamiliar
MemEMfamiliar
NenENfamiliar
OoOHrounded
PpePAYno strong puff of air
QkuKOO / KEWmostly in loanwords
RerERrolled/front or back-throat R
SesESfamiliar
TteTAYno strong puff of air
UuUUrounded lips, no exact English match
VveVAY / soft FAYoften softer than English V
WweWAY / soft V-WAYbetween English V and W
XiksIKSmostly in loanwords
YipsilonIP-see-lonmostly in loanwords
ZzetZETlike Z in "zip"

The IJ Combination ​

The letters I and J together (ij) are treated as a single "special Dutch letter" because they make one sound and are capitalized together in names like IJmuiden. Many learners think of ij as a 27th Dutch letter.

See: /shared/grammar/alphabet-pronunciation.md for more detail.

5. Grammar Reasoning ​

Why does Dutch pronunciation matter?

English spelling is historical and messy. Words like "knight," "psychology," and "through" don't follow clear rules. Dutch is different.

Dutch uses syllable structure to show how vowels sound:

  • A closed syllable ends in a consonant → single vowel is short: man (MAHN)
  • An open syllable ends in a vowel → single vowel is long: ma-ken (MAH-ken)
  • In a closed syllable, long vowels are written double: maan (MAHN = moon)

This system is so regular that once you learn the rules, you can read almost any Dutch word correctly. English speakers are used to guessing pronunciation; Dutch speakers rarely need to.

7. Pronunciation ​

Dutch pronunciation differs from English in several key ways:

Short Vowels (in closed syllables) ​

  • a sounds like "father": man (MAHN), tafel (TAH-fel)
  • e sounds like "bet": bed (BET), vet (VET)
  • i sounds like "sit": vis (VIS), kin (KIN)
  • o sounds like "off": bos (BOS), pot (POT)
  • u has NO exact English sound -- rounded lips: bus (BUUS), hut (HUT)

Long Vowels (in open syllables or doubled in closed syllables) ​

  • aa sounds like "father" held longer: maan (MAHN = moon)
  • ee sounds like "say" without the glide: been (BAYN = leg)
  • ii is rare; usually written as ie: fiets (FEETS = bicycle)
  • oo sounds like "oh" held: boom (BOHM = tree)
  • uu has no English sound -- rounded lips, held longer: muur (MUUR = wall)

Diphthongs (vowel combinations that glide) ​

  • ui (most difficult for English speakers): huis (HUYS = house) -- NOT "house," but rounded lips glide forward
  • ou sounds like "ow": koud (KOWT = cold)
  • au sounds like "ow" (same as ou): blauw (BLOW = blue)
  • ei sounds like "ay": klein (KLAYN = small)
  • ij sounds like "ay" (same as ei): mijn (MAYN = my)

Word Stress ​

Dutch usually stresses the first syllable of native words, but not always. Prefixes like be-, ge-, ver-, and ont- are typically unstressed.

  • TAH-fel (table): stress on first syllable
  • be-TAH-len (to pay): stress on second syllable (first is a prefix)
  • NAY-der-lants (Dutch language): stress on first syllable

8. Dialogue ​

This dialogue uses only alphabet and pronunciation concepts:

Leraar: Goedemorgen. Hoe gaat het?
Student: Goedemorgen. Het gaat goed.
Leraar: Wat is je naam?
Student: Ik heet Jan.
Leraar: Jan. Hoe spel je dat?
Student: J-A-N.
Leraar: Dank je wel. Welkom in Nederlands!

Translation:

Teacher: Good morning. How are you?
Student: Good morning. I'm doing well.
Teacher: What is your name?
Student: I'm called Jan.
Teacher: Jan. How do you spell that?
Student: J-A-N.
Teacher: Thank you. Welcome to Dutch!

9. Reading ​

Read this simple text aloud, paying attention to vowel length and stress:

De man ziet de maan. Het huis is klein. De fiets is blauw. De boom is hoog. Het water is koud.

Ik ben Jan. Ik leer Nederlands. De letters zijn moeilijk, maar het is goed.

English Translation:

The man sees the moon. The house is small. The bicycle is blue. The tree is tall. The water is cold.

I'm Jan. I'm learning Dutch. The letters are difficult, but it's good.

Pronunciation guide:

deh MAHN zeet deh MAHN / het HUYS is KLAYN / deh FEETS is BLOW / deh BOHM is HOHKH / het VAH-ter is KOWT

ik ben YAHN / ik layr NAY-der-lants / deh LET-ters zijin MOO-ay-lik, MAHR het is KHOOT

10. Listening ​

Listen to a native Dutch speaker read the following words aloud. As you listen, notice:

  • How short vowels vs. long vowels sound different
  • How word stress changes the rhythm
  • How diphthongs glide

(Audio would be located at /shared/assets/audio/A0-01-listening.mp3)

Transcript:

man / maan / bed / been / vis / fiets / bos / boom / bus / buur / huis / tuin / koud / blauw / klein / mijn / goed / gaan / hond / raam / rood / water / tafel / betalen / vertellen / Nederlands

Comprehension Questions:

  1. Which word sounds longer: man or maan?
  2. Which words have the "ow" sound (ou/au)?
  3. In the word "betalen," which syllable is stressed?

Answers: 1. maan 2. koud, blauw 3. second syllable (be-TAH-len)

11. Speaking ​

Practice pronouncing these words aloud. If you can, record yourself and compare to a native speaker.

Exercise 1: Read the alphabet

Say the Dutch letter names A through Z. Repeat until they feel natural.

Model Response: AH, BAY, SAY, DAY, AY, EF, KHAY, HAH, EE, YAY, KAH, EL, EM, EN, OH, PAY, KOO, ER, ES, TAY, UU, VAY, WAY, IKS, IP-see-lon, ZET

Exercise 2: Read word pairs (short vs. long vowels)

Read each pair aloud. Notice the vowel length difference.

  • man / maan
  • bed / been
  • vis / fiets
  • bos / boom
  • bus / buur

Exercise 3: Read diphthong words

Say each word, paying attention to the gliding sound:

  • huis (ui)
  • tuin (ui)
  • koud (ou)
  • blauw (au)
  • klein (ei)
  • mijn (ij)

Exercise 4: Read words with stress

Say each word, emphasizing the stressed syllable:

  • TAH-fel (table)
  • VAH-ter (water)
  • be-TAH-len (to pay)
  • ver-TEL-len (to tell)
  • NAY-der-lants (Dutch language)

12. Writing ​

Exercise 1: Match letters to sounds

Write down the Dutch letter name for each letter, then write a word that starts with it.

Example: A = ah, word: appel

Letters: B, G, J, U, R, W

Model Answers:

  • B = be, word: boom
  • G = ge, word: goed
  • J = je, word: ja
  • U = u, word: uw
  • R = er, word: rood
  • W = we, word: water

Exercise 2: Identify vowel length

Write "short" or "long" next to each word based on the vowel sound:

  1. man ___
  2. maan ___
  3. bed ___
  4. been ___
  5. bos ___
  6. boom ___

Answers: 1. short 2. long 3. short 4. long 5. short 6. long

Exercise 3: Diphthong sorting

Sort these words by diphthong type:

huis, klein, koud, mijn, blauw, tuin

  • ui words: ___
  • ij/ei words: ___
  • ou/au words: ___

Answers:

  • ui words: huis, tuin
  • ij/ei words: klein, mijn
  • ou/au words: koud, blauw

13. Common Mistakes ​

1. Saying Dutch g like English g

  • Wrong: huis with English g sound
  • Right: huis with back-of-throat sound (khuis)
  • Why: Dutch g comes from the back of the throat, like the "ch" in Scottish "loch"

2. Saying ui like English "house"

  • Wrong: HOUSE (hous)
  • Right: HUYS (with rounded lips, not spread lips)
  • Why: Dutch ui is a rounded diphthong; English "ow" is not rounded

3. Confusing ei and ij

  • Wrong: Thinking they sound different
  • Right: They sound the same in standard Dutch
  • Why: This is a spelling rule that must be memorized; pronunciation doesn't help

4. Treating ij as two letters

  • Wrong: EYE-JAY
  • Right: One sound: AY
  • Why: Dutch treats ij as a single letter unit for capitalization and pronunciation

5. Applying English stress to Dutch words

  • Wrong: PER-fect stress on every syllable equally
  • Right: One clear stressed syllable, unstressed syllables are light
  • Why: Dutch has strong stress-unstress contrast; English has weaker contrast

14. Dutch Insight ​

Dutch pronunciation frustrates English speakers because Dutch sounds don't always match English patterns. But this is actually good news: Dutch is more regular than English.

Once you master the vowel length rules and diphthong sounds, you can read almost any Dutch word. English has "tough," "through," and "though" -- three different pronunciations of the same letters. Dutch doesn't have this problem.

Also, Dutch speakers will almost always be patient with pronunciation mistakes. Dutch people speak many languages and understand that pronunciation is hard. Your goal is intelligibility, not perfection. Even native speakers vary slightly in how they pronounce certain sounds depending on region or personal habit.

15. Memory Tricks ​

1. The vowel length rule:

  • Closed syllable + single vowel = short: man, bed, vis, bus
  • Closed syllable + double vowel = long: maan, been, boom, buur
  • Think: "Double the vowel to make it long, like the vowel is stretching."

2. Diphthongs as combinations:

  • ui = "uh" + "ee" (rounded, gliding): huis
  • ei/ij = "eh" + "ee" (open, gliding): klein, mijn
  • ou/au = "aw" + "oo" (gliding): koud, blauw

3. Dutch g pronunciation:

  • Think: Back of throat. Say "back," then "loch" (Scottish), then Dutch "goed." Your throat is tightening. That's the Dutch g.

4. Word stress:

  • Native Dutch words: Usually first syllable (man, fiets, tafel)
  • Words with prefixes: Stress comes later (be-TAH-len, ver-TEL-len)
  • Think: Prefixes are unstressed; the real word gets the stress

16. Active Recall ​

Answer these questions without looking back. Then check your answers below.

  1. What are the THREE most difficult Dutch vowel sounds for English speakers?
  2. How do you know if a vowel is long or short in Dutch spelling?
  3. What sound does Dutch g make?
  4. Which diphthongs sound the same?
  5. In the word "betalen," which syllable gets the stress?

Answers:

  1. uu (rounded u with no English match), ui (rounded diphthong unlike English), Dutch g (throat sound unlike English g)
  2. In a closed syllable: double vowels = long, single vowels = short. In an open syllable: single vowels are long.
  3. A throat sound, like the "ch" in Scottish "loch" -- not like English "go"
  4. ei and ij sound the same; ou and au sound the same
  5. be-TAH-len (the prefix "be-" is unstressed)

17. Quiz ​

Read each question. Write your answer. Check your answer below. Aim for 80%+.

1. Which word has a SHORT vowel? A) maan
B) man
C) mijn
D) muur

2. In the word "fiets" (bicycle), what sound does the "ie" make? A) like English "foot"
B) like English "fee"
C) like English "fiat"
D) like English "fir"

3. Which diphthong requires rounded lips? A) au
B) ei
C) ui
D) ij

4. How do you spell the letter G in Dutch? A) GEE
B) JAY
C) GUH
D) GE

5. In the word "tafel" (table), which syllable is stressed? A) First syllable (TAH-)
B) Second syllable (-fel)
C) Both equally
D) Neither (it's flat)

6. Which word pair has the SAME vowel sound in Dutch? A) man / maan
B) bed / been
C) klein / mijn
D) ou / aw

7. What is the 27th "letter" of Dutch? A) uu
B) ij
C) ei
D) There is no 27th letter

8. In Dutch, the letters "ij" are capitalized as: A) Ij
B) iJ
C) IJ
D) iJ

9. The word "blauw" (blue) contains which diphthong? A) ui
B) ou
C) au
D) ei

10. Which sound does English NOT have that Dutch DOES? A) The "th" in "that"
B) The "ng" in "sing"
C) The "ch" sound in "loch" (Dutch g)
D) The "sh" in "show"

Answer Key:

  1. B -- man has a short vowel (single vowel in closed syllable)
  2. B -- ie sounds like English "fee" (FEETS)
  3. C -- ui requires rounded lips and is unique to Dutch
  4. D -- Dutch letter G is pronounced "ge" (KHAY)
  5. A -- tafel is stressed on the first syllable (TAH-fel)
  6. C -- klein and mijn both contain ei/ij, which sound the same
  7. B -- ij is treated as a single "Dutch letter" even though it's not official
  8. C -- ij is always capitalized together as IJ
  9. C -- blauw contains au (which sounds like ou)
  10. C -- Dutch g is a back-of-throat sound English speakers rarely use

18. Homework ​

Spend 30-40 minutes on this after finishing the lesson.

1. Alphabet Mastery (10 minutes)

  • Write out the Dutch alphabet A-Z with the Dutch letter names beside each
  • Record yourself saying the alphabet slowly
  • Listen back and notice which letters felt unnatural
  • Practice those letters 3 times

2. Vowel Pair Practice (10 minutes)

  • For each vowel pair below, say the short version, then the long version
  • Notice how the vowel changes quality, not just length
  • Pairs: a/aa, e/ee, i/ii (as ie), o/oo, u/uu
  • Say each pair 3 times

3. Diphthong Listening (10 minutes)

  • Listen to each diphthong word 3 times: huis, tuin, klein, mijn, koud, blauw
  • On the 3rd listening, try to repeat it aloud immediately after
  • Notice which ones feel awkward (probably ui)

4. Reading Practice (10 minutes)

  • Read the "Reading" section aloud slowly
  • Then read it at normal speed
  • Record yourself and listen back
  • Rate your pronunciation: 1 (terrible) to 5 (excellent)

Optional: Use a speech recognition app (Google Translate, Forvo, or YouTube) to check if native speakers understand your pronunciation.

19. Summary ​

Dutch spelling and pronunciation follow clear, regular rules. Unlike English, once you learn the rules, you can read almost any word correctly.

Key Takeaways:

  • Dutch uses the same 26 letters as English but with different names and sounds
  • Vowel length is shown by spelling: single vowel = short (man), double vowel = long (maan)
  • Diphthongs glide: ui, ei/ij, ou/au
  • Word stress usually falls on the first syllable of native Dutch words, but not always on words with prefixes
  • Dutch g is a back-of-throat sound, not English g

You now know:

  • ✓ The Dutch alphabet and how to pronounce each letter
  • ✓ How to distinguish short vs. long vowels by spelling
  • ✓ How to pronounce the major Dutch diphthongs
  • ✓ Where to place word stress
  • ✓ Why Dutch spelling is more regular than English

Next lesson: We'll move beyond sounds to your first real conversation -- how to introduce yourself in Dutch. You'll use the pronunciation foundation you've built to speak your first Dutch sentences.

To review: Repeat the alphabet daily. Read the "Reading" section aloud 2-3 times. Practice saying the diphthong words until they feel natural.
